details.description: Install a worker from a registry slug, an OCI image ref, or a LOCAL project directory (one containing an iii.worker.yaml). Call worker::schema to see each source shape, and worker::validate to dry-run an iii.worker.yaml before installing. LOCAL installs run the project directory LIVE and start a source watcher: code edits auto-restart the worker, so do NOT re-add after changing source files — re-add (force: true) only when iii.worker.yaml itself changes. Installs can outlive a bus invocation timeout and CONTINUE server-side — on timeout, poll worker::status instead of re-issuing (the project lock stays held until the in-flight install finishes).

WorkerSource.description: Where to fetch the worker from. Use `registry` for the public iii worker registry, `oci` for an arbitrary container image, or `local` for a filesystem path on the engine/daemon host (works over the trigger too; the path is resolved on the host, not the caller).

version.description: Optional pinned version (semver). Omit to take the latest stable.

path.description:
Path to a worker PROJECT DIRECTORY on the engine/daemon host (NOT the caller's machine), e.g. "/srv/workers/my-worker". The directory MUST contain an `iii.worker.yaml` manifest.

Minimal manifest (just name + how to start):
  name: my-worker
  scripts:
    start: "node src/index.js"

All iii.worker.yaml fields:
  name        (required) worker id; must be a single path segment (alphanumerics, '-', '_', '.').
  description (optional) one-line human/LLM-readable summary.
  scripts.start   (required unless inferred) command that runs the worker process.
  scripts.setup   (optional) one-time host provisioning, e.g. "apt-get install -y build-essential".
  scripts.install (optional) dependency install, e.g. "npm install".
  dependencies    (optional) map of other-worker-name -> semver range, e.g. { iii-state: "^0.19" }.
  resources.cpus   (optional) integer vCPUs, default 2.
  resources.memory (optional) MiB, default 2048.
  env             (optional) string->string vars injected into the worker (III_URL/III_ENGINE_URL are set by the engine and ignored here).
  runtime.base_image (optional) OCI rootfs override, e.g. "oven/bun:1".

Unknown keys are rejected at add time. The setup/install/start scripts run on the host. Works over the trigger as well as the CLI. Dry-run a manifest with `worker::validate`; fetch the full manifest JSON Schema via `worker::schema { function_id: "iii.worker.yaml" }`.

force.description: Force re-download by deleting cached artifacts before installing. Use to recover from a corrupt cache.

reset_config.description: Reset the worker's config.yaml block before re-adding. Combine with force=true for a clean reinstall.

wait.description: Block until the worker reports ready. Default true. Over the trigger surface installs routinely exceed bus invocation timeouts (npm install etc.) — prefer wait:false and poll worker::status. If a wait:true call times out, the install KEEPS RUNNING server-side: do not re-issue blindly (the project lock will be busy, W120); poll worker::status instead.

yes.description: Proceed without confirmation when a registry dependency graph contains more than 32 workers. Required for large-graph installs over the trigger or in non-interactive environments.

awaited_ready.description: Echoes `wait`. Does NOT confirm the worker is actually running — verify via worker::list.

config_path.description: Absolute path of the project config file the worker entry was written to.

status.description: Outcome status: installed (new), already_current, repaired, or replaced.

version.description: Installed version read from iii.lock. Null when the lockfile read failed; re-query via worker::list.

The `worker::add` contract: required `source`, optional `wait` (default true), `yes`, `force`, `reset_config`. For registry: `{ kind: "registry", name: "shell" }`.

Let me add the shell worker first with wait: true. Since it's already installed, the status should be `already_current` or similar. Let me do that.
Both workers are already installed and running, but the task requires adding each from the registry anyway, sequentially. Starting with `shell`:

Both add operations finished sequentially. Now step 2: "Invoke the dedicated code-file capability's own access-contract inspection operation. Generic engine function discovery does not satisfy this step."

This means calling `coder::info` — the dedicated code-file capability's own access-contract inspection operation (the coder access contract). I already have the description from the function list, but I should call `engine::functions::info` first? No — the step explicitly says "Invoke the dedicated code-file capability's own access-contract inspection operation" — that's `coder::info`. "Generic engine function discovery does not satisfy this step" means I can't just use `engine::functions::list` (which I already did) — I need to actually call `coder::info`.

Per my rules, I need to fetch the contract of `coder::info` before calling it (first call this session). Let me do that — actually, I can fetch the contract and then call. These are dependent (I should know the contract before calling), but I already have the description from the list. Still, rules say fetch contract before FIRST call. Let me fetch `coder::info` contract and then call it. Actually I can do both in sequence — fetch info first, then call. Let me fetch contracts for the coder functions I'll use: `coder::info`, `coder::create-file`, `coder::update-file`, `coder::move`, `coder::read-file`. I can fetch multiple at once with `{ function_ids: [...] }`. Then call `coder::info`.

Both registry adds completed sequentially. Now step 2 — invoke the code-file capability's own access-contract inspection (`coder::info`). First, let me fetch the contracts for the coder functions I'll use:

functions.description: Report the coder access contract: the effective mode (jailed = paths confined to the allowed roots; unjailed = deny-only, absolute paths anywhere on the host, roots anchor relative paths only), canonical allowed roots (primary first), the session_root that relative paths actually anchor against when the session is scoped (it overrides primary_root and may sit outside every allowed root), per-file size caps, response budgets (max_output_bytes, batch_read_budget_bytes, search_response_budget_bytes), listing/search limits, the non-accessible glob patterns, and the default_exclude_globs noise filter applied by tree/search. Call this FIRST when unsure where coder may read or write, or when a path was rejected — in jailed mode, paths outside every allowed root need the shell worker's shell::fs::* instead.

request_schema.description: No arguments — `coder::info` is a pure discovery call.
request_schema.title: InfoInput

AccessMode.description: Effective access mode of the coder surface — the same deny-only policy switch `shell::fs::*` runs under.

oneOf.description: Paths are confined to `base_paths`; anything outside is rejected.

Operator opt-in (`fs.allow_unjailed: true`, empty `fs.host_roots`): absolute paths anywhere on the host are accepted, confined only by `fs.denylist_paths` and `non_accessible_globs`. `base_paths` only anchor relative wire paths.

base_paths.description: Canonical absolute paths of the allowed roots, in configuration order. The primary root (index 0) is where relative wire paths resolve; an absolute path is accepted when it canonicalises inside ANY of these (in `unjailed` mode: anywhere on the host). In `jailed` mode paths outside every root are rejected — use `shell::fs::*` instead.

batch_read_budget_bytes.description: Aggregate budget across a single `paths[]` batch call to `coder::read-file`, measured in bytes of returned content (after UTF-8 sanitization — invalid bytes expand to U+FFFD before being counted, so the cap bounds what the caller actually receives). Entries are collected in request order; each entry may consume up to `min(remaining_budget, max_read_bytes)`. An entry reached with zero remaining budget receives a per-entry C218 naming this key, its value, and the bytes already consumed, with recovery guidance. Budget topology: batch reads are governed by this key; single-path full reads by `max_output_bytes`; windowed reads by `max_read_bytes` applied per returned window — `max_read_bytes` is also the per-file IO ceiling for all of them.

default_exclude_globs.description: Noise-exclusion globs (root-relative, same matching as `non_accessible_globs`): matching paths (node_modules, .git, …) are omitted from `coder::search` results and pruned from `coder::tree` descent — the directory surfaces as a childless `truncated` stub. Hide-only — no access protection. Pass `use_default_excludes: false` on those calls to look inside.

list_default_page_size.description: Default `page_size` used by `coder::list-folder` when the caller omits it.

max_output_bytes.description: Context budget for single-path FULL reads in `coder::read-file`, in bytes of returned content. Full reads larger than this return C218 with the file's size/line count and window/stat recovery guidance; a per-call `max_output_bytes` override is available on `coder::read-file` (clamped to `max_read_bytes`).

max_read_bytes.description: Per-file IO ceiling for `coder::read-file`. Full reads of files larger than this are rejected with C218; windowed reads cap the returned window bytes instead, so larger files stay readable window by window. Also the ceiling for `coder::search` content scanning — larger files are silently skipped during search.

max_write_bytes.description: Maximum bytes that `coder::create-file` or `coder::update-file` will accept for a single file write. Larger writes are rejected with C218.

mode.description: `jailed`: paths must stay inside `base_paths`. `unjailed`: absolute paths anywhere on the host are accepted (deny-only, like `shell::fs::*`) and `base_paths` only anchor relative paths.

non_accessible_globs.description: Glob patterns matched per root (root-relative). Files whose root-relative path matches are listable but not readable/writable/deletable/creatable; they return C211.

primary_root.description: Convenience duplicate of `base_paths[0]` — the primary allowed root. Relative paths resolve against this directory UNLESS `session_root` is set, which takes precedence.

search_default_max_line_bytes.description: Per-line byte cap in `coder::search`: matching considers at most this many bytes of each line, and matched/context lines are truncated to it.

search_default_max_matches.description: Default `max_matches` used by `coder::search` when the caller omits it.

search_response_budget_bytes.description: Aggregate byte budget for one `coder::search` response, measured in payload bytes (paths + matched text + context lines). When the budget is hit the response sets `truncated: true` — refine the query or add `include_globs`.

session_root.description: The session's working directory when the caller runs under a harness-stamped filesystem scope; `null` otherwise. When set, THIS is what relative wire paths (and `coder::search` glob matching) anchor against — not `primary_root`. In `unjailed` mode it may sit outside every `base_paths` entry, so a relative path that looks wrong against the allowed roots can still be correct here. Check it first when a relative path was rejected.

tree_default_depth.description: Default `max_depth` used by `coder::tree` when the caller omits it.

tree_per_folder_limit.description: Maximum entries returned per folder node by `coder::tree`; folders that exceed this are flagged `truncated`.

functions.description: Create one or more files. Request shape: {"files": [{"path": "...", "content": "..."}]}. Per-file `overwrite` and `parents` flags; non-accessible paths return C211. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

mode.description: Octal permission bits as a string, e.g. "0644". Defaults to "0644".

overwrite.description: When false (the default), refuse to write if `path` already exists.

parents.description: Create missing parent directories. Defaults to true so a single `coder::create-file` call can scaffold a fresh subtree.

path.description: Path relative to the primary allowed root, or an absolute path inside any allowed root. Call `coder::info` to see the allowed roots. Paths outside every allowed root are rejected — use the shell worker's `shell::fs::*` for host paths outside the jail.

error.description: Structured error for this entry. `code` is stable for programmatic branching (e.g. `"C213"` means already-exists; pass `overwrite=true` to replace). `message` carries the corrective action an LLM agent needs to make a successful second call.

path.description: Canonical absolute path (resolved through the jail); the caller's input verbatim when resolution failed.

WireError.description:
Structured per-entry error as it appears on the wire.

Use `code` for stable programmatic branching (e.g. `"C211"` for not-found-or-denied). `message` carries the human/LLM-readable problem description plus the corrective next call.

code.description: Stable error code, e.g. "C211". See the README error table.

message.description: Human/LLM-readable message: problem + actual values + corrective next call.

functions.description: Apply batched line-oriented and regex edits across one or more files. Request shape: {"files": [{"path": "...", "ops": [...]}]}. Line ops: { op: 'insert', at_line, content } | { op: 'remove', from_line, to_line } | { op: 'update_lines', from_line, to_line, content } — 1-based, inclusive, applied bottom-up. Regex op: { op: 'replace', pattern, replacement, ignore_case?, dot_matches_newline?, expect_matches? } runs on the file body after line ops. Replace large regions WITHOUT quoting them: two short anchors joined by .*? with dot_matches_newline: true — always prefer wildcards over pasting the block into the pattern. expect_matches: 1 turns a silent multi-site clobber into a safe pre-write C210; expect_matches: 0 asserts absence. In `replacement`, $1/${name} are capture references and a literal $ must be written $$ (JS/TS template literals: `Hello, $${name}!`); undefined references fail pre-write with C210. Each file commits atomically via temp + rename. On success each applied line op returns a bounded post-apply echo (±2 context lines); regex replace ops return up to 5 per-match-site echoes (first + last line of each replaced region, inner lines elided) — verify from the echoes instead of re-reading the file. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*.

path.description: Path relative to the primary allowed root, or an absolute path inside any allowed root. Call `coder::info` to see the allowed roots. Paths outside every allowed root are rejected — use the shell worker's `shell::fs::*` for host paths outside the jail.

oneOf.description: Insert `content` before line `at_line` (1-based). `at_line = lines+1` appends to end of file.
Delete lines `from_line..=to_line` (1-based, inclusive).
Overwrite lines `from_line..=to_line` with `content`.
Replace all regex matches in the file body (after line ops).

dot_matches_newline.description: When true, `.` in `pattern` also matches `\n`, so a short anchored pattern like `"fn parse_config\\(.*?\\n\\}"` replaces a whole multi-line region without quoting it — prefer two short anchors joined by `.*?` over pasting the block into the pattern. Without this flag (the default), `.` does not cross newlines and a multi-line pattern silently matches nothing.

expect_matches.description: Expected number of matches for this op. When set and the actual count differs, this FILE fails with C210 and nothing is written to it (other files in the batch still apply). Set `expect_matches: 1` to make a targeted read-free edit safe — a mismatch means the pattern is anchored too loosely or matches nothing. Set `expect_matches: 0` to assert ABSENCE: the op succeeds only when nothing matches (the replacement is unused). Omit to replace all matches unconditionally.

replacement.description: Substitution text for each match. Capture references expand: `$1`/`${1}` by index (`$0` is the whole match) and `$name`/`${name}` by name. A literal `$` MUST be written `$$` — JS/TS template literals in a replacement are the classic collision: write `Hello, $${name}!` to output `Hello, ${name}!`. Unbraced references consume the longest `[0-9A-Za-z_]` run, so `$1a` means a group named "1a", NOT group 1 then "a" (use `${1}a`). A reference to a group the pattern does not define fails pre-write with C210 — nothing is written. References are validated even when the replacement goes unused (e.g. `expect_matches: 0`): the replacement must be well-formed even when unused.

OpEcho.description: Post-apply snapshot of the region affected by one op. Line ops echo the affected region with ±2 context lines; regex `replace` ops emit one echo per match site (up to 5, no context): the FIRST and LAST line of the post-replace region, with `elided` set to the inner line count when the region spans more than 2 lines (single-line replacements echo just that line). Each site carries `total_replacements`. Provides just enough context to verify the edit landed in the right place without flooding the LLM context with the full file body.

elided.description: Number of middle lines elided from a large region: for line ops, set when the affected region exceeded the per-echo cap; for replace sites, the count of inner lines between the region's echoed first and last line (set when the region spans >2 lines).

from_line.description: 1-based line number of the first echoed line (after all ops applied).

lines.description: The echoed lines, post-apply. When the region is large, middle lines are elided and `elided` is set to indicate how many were skipped.

op_index.description: Index of the op in the request's ops array (0-based).

total_replacements.description: Total number of replacements the regex op made across the whole file (set only on replace-op site echoes, duplicated on each site). Sites are capped at 5 — when more matched, this count is the only record of the extras.

applied.description: Number of operations applied (only meaningful when `success`).

echoes.description: Per-op bounded post-apply echoes for edit verification; each applied op returns a snapshot of the affected region (±2 context lines) so the caller can confirm the edit landed at the right position without receiving the full file body. See `OpEcho` for field semantics. Empty on failure. Always present on the wire.

echoes_truncated.description: True when the total echo budget (~4 KiB) was exhausted before all op echoes could be emitted. Use `coder::read-file` to inspect the full result if needed. Always present on the wire.

error.description: Structured error for this entry. `code` is stable for programmatic branching (e.g. `"C211"` for not-found-or-denied; `"C210"` for bad input such as overlapping ops). `message` carries the corrective action an LLM agent needs to make a successful second call.

new_line_count.description: Final line count after applying (only meaningful when `success`).

path.description: Canonical absolute path (resolved through the jail); the caller's input verbatim when resolution failed.

WireError.description:
Structured per-entry error as it appears on the wire.

Use `code` for stable programmatic branching (e.g. `"C211"` for not-found-or-denied). `message` carries the human/LLM-readable problem description plus the corrective next call.

code.description: Stable error code, e.g. "C211". See the README error table.

message.description: Human/LLM-readable message: problem + actual values + corrective next call.

functions.description: Move or rename one or more paths inside the jail. Request shape: {"files": [{"from": "...", "to": "..."}]}. Paths are relative to the primary allowed root or absolute inside any allowed root (coder::info lists them); for host paths outside the jail use shell::fs::*. Per-entry `overwrite` and `parents` flags. Same-root moves use a per-file-atomic rename; cross-root moves use copy+delete (files only — cross-root directory moves are unsupported, move files individually). Copy+delete is rollback-safe: if source deletion fails after a successful copy the copy is removed and the error names the failure; if rollback also fails the error names both states for manual cleanup.

from.description: Source path: relative to the primary allowed root, or an absolute path inside any allowed root. Call `coder::info` to see the allowed roots. Paths outside every allowed root are rejected — use the shell worker's `shell::fs::*` for host paths outside the jail.

overwrite.description: When false (the default), refuse to overwrite an existing destination. Pass `overwrite: true` to replace an existing file at `to`.

parents.description: Create missing parent directories of the destination. Defaults to true.

to.description: Destination path: relative to the primary allowed root, or an absolute path inside any allowed root. Call `coder::info` to see the allowed roots. Paths outside every allowed root are rejected — use the shell worker's `shell::fs::*` for host paths outside the jail.

files.description: Entries to move. Each entry is processed independently so a single failure never aborts the rest.

error.description: Structured error for this entry. `code` is stable for programmatic branching (e.g. `"C213"` means destination exists; pass `overwrite=true` to replace; `"C210"` for disallowed operations such as cross-root directory moves, moving a root itself, or a destination that is a directory — the message then names the corrected target path). `message` carries the corrective action an LLM agent needs to make a successful second call.

from.description: Canonical absolute path of the source (resolved through the jail); the caller's input verbatim when resolution failed.

moved.description: True only when the move fully completed; false for a no-op self-move (`from` and `to` resolve to the same file).

to.description: Canonical absolute path of the destination (resolved through the jail); the caller's input verbatim when resolution failed.

WireError.description:
Structured per-entry error as it appears on the wire.

Use `code` for stable programmatic branching (e.g. `"C211"` for not-found-or-denied). `message` carries the human/LLM-readable problem description plus the corrective next call.

path.description: File to read. Same jail rules as the top-level `path` field.

line_from.description: First line of the window, 1-based inclusive (must be >= 1; 0 is rejected with C210). Setting `line_from` and/or `line_to` switches to windowed mode: the file is streamed and only the requested lines are returned, so files larger than `max_read_bytes` stay readable slice by slice — the byte cap then applies to the returned window, never the file size. Defaults to 1 when only `line_to` is set. A window starting past EOF succeeds with empty content and reports the file's `total_lines`. Lines are 0x0A- or EOF-terminated segments; a trailing newline does not create a phantom line (same convention as `coder::update-file`).

line_to.description: Last line of the window, 1-based inclusive. Must be >= `line_from` (C210 otherwise). Omit to read from `line_from` to end-of-file (still bounded by `max_read_bytes` on the returned bytes). Only valid in single-path mode (`path`); ignored when `paths` is set.

max_output_bytes.description: Per-call override of the `max_output_bytes` config (default 131072) that budgets single-path FULL reads, measured in returned content bytes after UTF-8 conversion (numbered prefixes included). Values above `max_read_bytes` are silently clamped to it. When the full content would exceed the effective budget the call fails with a C218 naming the file's size and `total_lines` — recover by windowing with `line_from`/`line_to`, probing with `stat: true`, or raising this field. Full reads only: combining it with `line_from`/`line_to` is C210 (windows are bounded by `max_read_bytes` instead); ignored when `paths` is set (batch mode is governed by `batch_read_budget_bytes`).

numbered.description: When true every returned content line is prefixed `N→`, where N is the line's ABSOLUTE 1-based number in the file — a window starting at `line_from: 40` is numbered from 40, not 1. Numbers match `coder::update-file`'s 1-based line ops exactly, so you can go from a numbered read straight to a line edit. Prefix bytes count toward all byte caps and budgets (no hidden bypass). path.description: Single file to read. Relative to the primary allowed root, or an absolute path inside any allowed root. Call `coder::info` to see the allowed roots. Paths outside every allowed root are rejected — use the shell worker's `shell::fs::*` for host paths outside the jail. Mutually exclusive with `paths` (XOR): pass either `path` or `paths`, not both — C210 if both or neither is set.

paths.description: Batch of files (or windowed slices) to read in a single call. Each entry is either a plain path string (whole-file read) or an object `{path, line_from?, line_to?}` with per-entry window parameters. Entries are processed in request order against a shared `batch_read_budget_bytes` cap, measured in bytes of returned content (after UTF-8 sanitization) — see `coder::info` for the configured value. Results are returned in the `results` field; top-level fields are null. Mutually exclusive with `path` (XOR): pass either `path` or `paths`, not both — C210 if both or neither is set.

stat.description: Metadata probe — the cheap "how big is it" call. When true the response carries size/mode/mtime plus `total_lines` and `is_utf8` (both null when the file exceeds `max_read_bytes` — size/mode/mtime still populate, so stat on a huge file SUCCEEDS); `content` is null, `lines_returned` 0, `more_lines` false. Probe BEFORE reading an unknown file, then fetch just the slice you need with `line_from`/`line_to`. Mutually exclusive with `line_from`, `line_to`, `numbered`, and `max_output_bytes` (C210 — stat returns no content for them to act on). Batch entries take a per-entry `stat` field instead; this top-level flag is ignored when `paths` is set.

ReadEntryResult.description: Per-entry result in a batch `paths[]` response.

content.description: File content as a UTF-8 string — the whole file or the requested window. Binary bytes are replaced by U+FFFD (`is_utf8: false`). `null` on failure.

error.description: Structured error — present only when `success: false`.

is_utf8.description: Whether `content` survived UTF-8 conversion without losing bytes. `null` on failure.

lines_returned.description: Number of lines returned in `content`. `null` on failure.

mode.description: Unix permission bits (lower 9 bits of `st_mode`), e.g. 0o644. `null` on failure.

more_lines.description: `true` when the file has content beyond what `content` includes (window ended before EOF, or byte budget cut the window short). `null` on failure.

mtime.description: Last-modified time as a Unix epoch in seconds. `null` on failure.

path.description: Canonical absolute path of the file (resolved through the jail). If resolution failed, this echoes the caller's input verbatim.

size.description: Size of the FILE in bytes (from metadata). `null` on failure or when the entry budget was exhausted before the file was opened.

success.description: `true` when the read succeeded (content/metadata fields are populated); `false` when an error occurred (only `error` is set).

total_lines.description: Total lines in the file; present when the stream reached EOF during this entry's read. `null` when not traversed or on failure.

content.text:
You are advising a five-engineer team that operates a payments ledger service on a single PostgreSQL instance. Facts: storage sits at 70% of the current instance's capacity, and one larger instance size (double the capacity) is still available from the cloud provider; data volume doubles roughly every eight months; about 60% of stored rows are reconciliation records older than 18 months that are read only during audits; regulators require strict transactional consistency for ledger writes; nobody on the team has operated a sharded or distributed database; leadership expects entry into two new markets within twelve months, which may double merchant count.

The team must commit now to one of two plans: (A) shard PostgreSQL by merchant id over the next two quarters, or (B) stay single-node, move audit-only records to cheaper archival storage, take the instance upgrade when needed, and re-evaluate in twelve months.

Recommend exactly one option. Justify it against the stated facts, state the real costs and risks of the option you recommend, and give concrete conditions under which the other option would become the right choice. Answer in a single reply and do not perform any external action.

The user asks for a recommendation between Plan A (shard PostgreSQL by merchant id) and Plan B (stay single-node, archive old records, upgrade instance, re-evaluate in 12 months). This is a pure advisory question — no external action needed. "Answer in a single reply and do not perform any external action."

So I should just answer. No tool calls needed. Let me think carefully about the substance.

Facts:
- Storage at 70% of current capacity.
- One larger instance size available (double capacity).
- Data volume doubles roughly every 8 months (~1.5x per year... actually doubling every 8 months means ~2.6x per year).
- ~60% of stored rows are reconciliation records older than 18 months, read only during audits.
- Regulators require strict transactional consistency for ledger writes.
- Nobody on the team has operated a sharded or distributed database.
- Leadership expects entry into two new markets within 12 months, may double merchant count.

Plan A: shard PostgreSQL by merchant id over next two quarters (6 months).
Plan B: stay single-node, move audit-only records to cheaper archival storage, take instance upgrade when needed, re-evaluate in 12 months.

Recommendation: Plan B.

Justification:
- The actual constraint is storage, not throughput/compute. Storage at 70% — but 60% of rows are old reconciliation records that can be archived. Archiving those immediately frees ~40%+ of capacity (60% of rows archived means storage drops from 70% to roughly 28% if the archived records are the bulk). Then the instance upgrade doubles capacity, giving headroom for years given data doubling every 8 months.
- Timeline math: data doubles every ~8 months. Even without archiving: 70% used now. With archiving, drop to ~28%. Upgrade to double capacity → effective ~14% of new capacity used. Doubling every 8 months: 14% → 28% at 8 months → 56% at 16 months → 112% at 24 months. So ~16-20 months of headroom even without further archiving, and archiving is ongoing, so much longer. Actually let's compute: after archiving, usage ~28% of current instance; upgraded instance is 2x so 14% of new. Doubling every 8 months: 14, 28, 56, 112 — crosses 100% between month 16 and 24. That's well past the 12-month re-evaluation horizon. With continued archival as records age past 18 months, the growth rate of "hot" storage is much lower.
- Sharding is a huge operational undertaking: distributed transactions, cross-shard queries, id routing, resharding as data grows, no team experience. For a payments ledger with strict transactional consistency requirements, sharding by merchant id breaks cross-merchant transactions (e.g., merchant payouts, funds movement across merchants, reconciliation aggregates). Regulators require strict consistency for ledger writes — a naive shard by merchant id risks cross-shard consistency problems.
- The real driver is merchant count doubling (two new markets), not necessarily per-merchant data explosion. Sharding by merchant id when the concern is onboarding more merchants doesn't help if the bottleneck is storage; it adds a second bottleneck (operational complexity) without addressing storage if storage growth is per-merchant data.
- The team has no distributed database experience — the two-quarter sharding timeline is optimistic; real migrations take longer, and a botched ledger migration is catastrophic (audit, regulatory risk).
- Plan B costs: archival engineering (ETL pipeline, storage costs, audit-retrieval path), instance upgrade cost (double cost), re-evaluation in 12 months. These are modest, incremental, reversible.
- Plan B risks: eventually hitting a ceiling (compute or storage) if growth exceeds projections; audit retrieval latency from cold storage; single point of failure remains; need to ensure archival pipeline correctness (transactional consistency of the archive, regulators may require integrity of archived records).
- Conditions where Plan A becomes right: growth accelerates beyond doubling every 8 months (e.g., data volume tripling yearly after new markets land); throughput/compute becomes the bottleneck (not just storage) — e.g., write volume or query load exceeds single-node capacity even after archiving and upgrade; need for geographic/regulatory data residency requiring separate deployments; per-merchant data grows so large that the largest merchant's data alone approaches single-node limits; team gains experience or hires distributed-systems expertise; cross-merchant transactional scope can be reduced (e.g., design changes confine transactions within a merchant); regulatory requirement changes force data segregation.

Also conditions under which A is right: if after 12 months the re-evaluation shows the largest-merchant data alone would exceed a single instance, or if total hot data outgrows largest instance available from provider (the "one larger size" is finite — there's a ceiling: only one bigger size available; eventually you run out of vertical headroom). Actually key point: provider only has ONE larger size (double). After that, no more vertical scaling — that's the real long-run ceiling. But at current growth, the upgraded instance lasts ~2 years; re-evaluation at 12 months will give updated data to decide whether to start sharding (which is a 2-quarter+ project) before hitting the ceiling. So B buys time to plan A properly with real data and possibly training.

Also mention: sharding by merchant id conflicts with the 60% reconciliation records — those are cross-merchant by nature (reconciliation across the whole ledger), so archiving them is orthogonal and needed regardless. Actually reconciliation records being read only during audits means they're a storage problem, not a hot-path problem — archive them regardless of plan; even in plan A you'd archive them. So B's archival step is needed in both plans.

Costs of B:
- Build and maintain archival pipeline (moving 60% of rows to S3/cold storage), including integrity/audit-retrieval tooling; engineers' time; potential latency for audit retrievals (minutes vs ms); storage cost of cold tier (cheap but not free); risk of archive pipeline bugs (data loss → regulatory issue); double instance cost (~2x compute bill) when upgrade happens; single point of failure remains (availability risk).
- Risk: if growth is actually faster than modeled, you might need the upgrade sooner and might approach the vertical ceiling before 12 months; audit reads from cold storage can be slow; you remain on one node so a hardware failure is an outage (though that's true in A too unless replicated).

Costs of A (to state as why not, briefly): massive engineering cost over two quarters: sharding middleware or Citus, repartitioning live data, cross-shard transaction handling, query fan-out, resharding later, training/ops burden, migration risk to a regulated ledger, and shard-by-merchant breaks cross-merchant transactions which the reconciliation/audit world needs. Also it doesn't even fix the storage problem if growth is dominated by archive-class records — you'd still archive.

Concrete conditions for A to be right:
1. After 12-month re-eval: hot (non-archivable) data growth projects to exceed the largest available single instance within ~18 months (i.e., you're about to hit the vertical ceiling; the "one larger size" is exhausted).
2. Write/query throughput, not storage, becomes the binding constraint even after archiving — e.g., peak transaction rates exceed single-node capability.
3. Data volume growth accelerates materially (e.g., >2x every 6 months) as new markets land, faster than archival can offset.
4. Largest single merchant's data alone approaches instance limits (shard key works: big merchants get their own shards).
5. Team gains/ hires distributed DB expertise or adopts a managed sharded offering (Citus/Aurora) to de-risk.
6. Regulatory requirements demand data residency/segregation that forces multiple deployments anyway.
7. Cross-merchant transaction scope can be shrunk (e.g., reconciliation moved fully off the OLTP ledger) so shard-by-merchant doesn't break consistency requirements.

Recommendation: B.

Keep it structured: Recommendation; Justification vs facts; Costs & risks of B; Conditions where A becomes right. Keep reasonably concise but complete. Length: moderate — this is an advisory deliverable, a few hundred words, well structured. Maybe 450-600 words. Use headers or bold. Avoid over-formatting. No tool calls.

## Recommendation: Plan B — stay single-node, archive, upgrade when needed, re-evaluate in 12 months

**Recommended.** Plan B addresses the actual constraint, is reversible and low-risk, and preserves the option to do Plan A properly later with real data. Plan A spends two quarters of engineering on a high-risk migration that doesn't even fix the dominant problem.

## Justification against the stated facts

1. **The binding constraint is storage, not throughput or scale.** Storage sits at 70%, and 60% of rows are audit-only reconciliation records. Archiving those immediately drops usage to roughly 28% of current capacity — before any upgrade. The instance upgrade (2× capacity) then puts effective usage at ~14% of the new size. At 2× growth every 8 months, that's ~16–20 months of headroom **even if nothing else is archived**, and archival is ongoing, so the runway is longer. That comfortably covers the 12-month re-evaluation window.
2. **Sharding doesn't solve the storage problem anyway.** The dominant storage consumer is archive-class, cross-merchant reconciliation data. You'd archive it under Plan A too. Sharding by merchant id addresses hot-path scale, which the facts don't show is the problem — the new markets double *merchant count*, not necessarily per-merchant data.
3. **Sharding by merchant id collides with the regulatory constraint.** Regulators require strict transactional consistency for ledger writes. Shard-by-merchant breaks cross-merchant transactions (payouts, fund movements, reconciliation aggregates), forcing distributed transactions, fan-out queries, and id routing — exactly the failure modes a team with **no distributed-database experience** will get wrong, on a regulated payments ledger where a botched migration is catastrophic. A two-quarter timeline for this with a zero-experience team is optimistic to the point of being a schedule risk.
4. **Plan B is incremental and reversible.** Archival and an instance upgrade are well-understood, low-risk operations. The "one larger size" is a finite vertical ceiling, but at modeled growth it isn't reached for ~2 years — Plan B buys time to staff up, gather real post-market data, and *then* run a properly resourced sharding project before hitting the ceiling.

## Real costs and risks of Plan B

- **Engineering cost:** building and maintaining the archival pipeline (extract ~60% of rows to cold/object storage with integrity checks), plus audit-retrieval tooling. The pipeline must be provably correct — a bug that silently drops archived records is a regulatory incident.
- **Operational costs:** the 2× instance bill when the upgrade lands; cold-tier storage fees; audit retrievals go from milliseconds to minutes.
- **Risks:** the growth model is wrong and demand accelerates faster than archival offsets, forcing the upgrade early and approaching the vertical ceiling sooner than modeled; the single node remains a single point of failure (availability risk — though Plan A as scoped doesn't fix that either); audit-read latency from archival.

## Conditions under which Plan A becomes the right choice

Switch to sharding (ideally as a properly resourced project, not a two-quarter squeeze) when any of these hold:

1. **The vertical ceiling comes into view:** after the 12-month re-evaluation, hot (non-archivable) data projects to exceed the largest available single instance within ~18 months.
2. **Throughput, not storage, becomes the binding constraint** — peak write/query rates exceed single-node capability even after archiving and the upgrade.
3. **Growth accelerates materially** — new markets drive >2× volume every ~6 months, faster than archival can offset.
4. **A single large merchant's data alone approaches instance limits** (shard key then actually works: big merchants get dedicated shards).
5. **The team gains distributed-DB experience or adopts a managed sharded offering** (e.g., Citus/Aurora), removing the biggest execution risk.
6. **Regulators require data residency/segregation** that forces multiple deployments anyway.
7. **Cross-merchant transactional scope shrinks** (e.g., reconciliation moves fully off the OLTP ledger), so shard-by-merchant no longer breaks the consistency requirement.

None of these conditions are indicated by the stated facts today. Commit to B, archive now, upgrade when utilization warrants, and let the 12-month data decide whether A's conditions have arrived.

After archiving and taking the 2× upgrade, live data sits at ~14% of the new instance's capacity and doubles every ~8 months — roughly two years of headroom even without tightening the archive cadence. The 12-month re-evaluation point lands with margin to spare.

3. **Strict transactional consistency + no distributed-DB experience makes A the highest-risk option on the table.** A merchant-id shard boundary does not respect the ledger's real transaction boundaries: settlements, cross-merchant transfers, chargebacks, batch reconciliation, and global reporting all cross shards. Those require distributed transactions (2PC or sagas), idempotency across shards, rebalancing, and new failure modes — precisely where regulatory consistency guarantees break. A team that has never operated a sharded database attempting this on a payments ledger in two quarters is a compliance incident waiting to happen.

4. **The market expansion is "may," and merchant count ≠ data volume.** Doubling merchants does not double transaction rows unless per-merchant volume also doubles, and even a 2× volume shock fits the post-archive single node within the window. This is a scenario to model, not a forcing function.

5. **B uses skills the team already has** (archival pipeline, instance upgrade, backup/restore). A demands skills nobody on the team possesses, on a regulated system, on a deadline.

## Real costs and risks of B

- **The archive must be done right, or it fails its purpose.** It must be immutable, integrity-verifiable, retention-compliant, and queryable within an audit SLA with a reliable retrieval path. A slow or non-compliant audit story is a real regulatory cost.
- **Backfill risk.** Moving 60% of rows safely requires proving they are terminal — no live write references them — and handling FK/reference edges so archival never breaks ledger consistency.
- **Upgrade risk.** The 2× instance move has downtime/rollback implications; it must be rehearsed. It also buys ~2 years, not forever.
- **Deferred-migration risk — the honest one.** If A eventually becomes necessary, doing it later means moving more data and having less runway. Mitigation: the archive shrinks the data that would ever need sharding, and the 12-month checkpoint becomes a hard gate with written criteria, not a vague intention.
- **Estimation risk.** Two new markets could surprise on volume. Define triggers now — e.g., hot storage exceeding ~65% of current instance, sustained IO/latency degradation, or per-merchant volume growth outpacing the model — to upgrade or re-evaluate early rather than at month 12.

## When A becomes the right choice

- **The archive + largest-instance upgrade stop being enough.** If the re-evaluation projects capacity exhaustion in under ~12–18 months even with archiving — because hot data grows faster than modeled, or the archive-eligible fraction shrinks (e.g., regulators lengthen retention or audits need recent reconciliation hot).
- **The ceiling is hit on something other than storage:** connection counts, IOPS, or compute — the point where vertical scaling plateaus. That is the real trigger for distribution, not the 70% storage number.
- **Regulation demands geographic distribution** (data residency), which a single instance cannot satisfy.
- **The team gains distributed-DB capability** — a hire, or adoption of Postgres-compatible managed sharding (e.g., Citus), which preserves SQL semantics and shrinks the consistency risk. If that path is taken, prefer incremental migration (new merchants onto new shards, hot merchants moved later) over a two-quarter big-bang shard.
- **Archiving is infeasible for compliance reasons** — then B's main lever disappears and A becomes the only storage-relief path, to be planned carefully regardless of team experience.

Commit to B now, build the archive as the priority deliverable, set the numeric triggers for upgrade and re-evaluation, and treat month 12 as a decision point with pre-agreed criteria — not a hope.

Let me think through the actual substance carefully.

Facts:
- Payments ledger service on single PostgreSQL instance
- Storage at 70% of current capacity
- One larger instance size (2x capacity) available
- Data volume doubles roughly every 8 months
- ~60% of stored rows are reconciliation records older than 18 months, read only during audits
- Regulators require strict transactional consistency for ledger writes
- Nobody has operated a sharded/distributed database

A) Shard PostgreSQL by merchant id over next two quarters
B) Stay single-node, archive audit-only records, upgrade instance when needed, re-evaluate in 12 months

Recommend exactly one. Justify against facts, state real costs/risks of the recommended option, give conditions under which the other becomes right.

My recommendation: B. Stay single-node with archival + upgrade, re-evaluate.

Reasons:
1. Storage math: 70% used now. Doubling every 8 months. But 60% of rows are audit-only records older than 18 months. Archiving those to cheaper storage would drop storage dramatically — roughly 60% of rows removed → storage falls well below 50%. That buys a lot of time even without the upgrade. And the upgrade doubles capacity when needed. So the storage pressure that looks urgent is mostly an archiving problem, not a scale problem.

2. The real bottleneck is likely not storage anyway — it's transactional consistency requirements for ledger writes. Sharding by merchant id would put cross-merchant transactions at risk; any transaction touching multiple merchants becomes a distributed transaction (2PC), which is exactly what regulators' strict consistency requirement makes painful. Payments ledgers often need global invariants (e.g., settlement totals, inter-merchant transfers, reporting). Sharding by merchant id makes those hard.

3. Team capability: no one has operated a sharded/distributed DB. Sharding PostgreSQL (e.g., Citus) over two quarters with a five-person team that has zero distributed-DB experience, while running a payments service under regulatory scrutiny, is a huge risk. Two quarters is aggressive for a migration like that, and the team would be learning on production money movement.

4. The two new markets may double merchant count, but merchant count ≠ data volume per merchant necessarily; even if it doubles data volume, that's still within the archiving + one upgrade headroom. The workload is likely still fine on a single node. Data volume doubling every 8 months, with 60% archived away, means the growth curve flattens substantially.

5. Sharding is also largely orthogonal to storage: sharding by merchant doesn't reduce total data, it spreads it. If the goal is storage relief, archiving is the direct fix. Sharding helps CPU/IO scaling and per-shard size, but at 70% capacity the immediate lever is archive.

Costs/risks of B:
- Must actually do the archiving work: build a pipeline, ensure audit retrieval path works (the data must remain queryable during audits — read-only but retrievable), handle regulatory retention requirements (archival storage still must be durable, immutable/append-only, retrievable within audit timelines). Risk: regulatory retention specs, retrieval SLAs.
- Instance upgrade causes downtime or at least a failover/restart — plan for maintenance window; PostgreSQL upgrades (instance size change) may need careful handling of connections, bloat, vacuum. Real cost: a maintenance window, possibly brief downtime.
- Operational risk: running closer to capacity limits; need monitoring, bloat management (VACUUM), connection limits; 70% → archive → maybe 30-40%, so headroom is comfortable.
- Re-evaluation cost: the 12-month deferral means the sharding project, if eventually needed, starts later; but the team can spend the next 12 months learning (read about Citus, run a pilot in staging) — actually that's a plus: they can de-risk option A during the year.
- If growth exceeds expectations (e.g., new markets drive far more than 2x, or write throughput becomes the bottleneck), single node hits a wall; the upgrade only doubles capacity once, and after that they're back at the decision point under more time pressure.
- Cost of upgrade: cloud spend roughly doubles; archival storage adds cost but much cheaper per GB; net probably still cheaper than sharding ops overhead.

Conditions under which A becomes right:
- Write throughput (TPS) becomes the binding constraint, not storage — sharding distributes writes.
- Data volume grows faster than projected (e.g., >2x in 8 months sustained, or new markets massively increase volume per merchant).
- They exhaust the instance size ladder (need >2x and it's the top, or next size is a big price jump).
- Reporting/analytics queries degrade because of the archive (if auditors/reporting need the archived data in hot storage frequently).
- The team gains distributed-DB experience (hired or trained) and can run a pilot.
- Regulatory change requires global consistency that actually can't be met with eventual consistency — interestingly, that argues for staying single node, but if they MUST shard, they need a solution with strong consistency (e.g., Citus with proper coordination, or partition by merchant but design transactions to be single-merchant).
- If the 12-month re-evaluation shows sustained 2x-per-8-months growth with no archiving relief left and CPU/IO saturation.

Also worth noting: even under A, they'd still want archiving (sharding doesn't remove the 60% audit rows problem — it just spreads them). So B is a prerequisite-ish step either way. And sharding by merchant id is a specific, limited shard key that fails for cross-merchant operations — better options might be partitioning by time (native PostgreSQL partitioning) first, which is much simpler and doesn't require distributed ops. I can mention partitioning as a middle step but the question forces a binary choice between A and B, so recommend B.

Should I mention that B includes possible native table partitioning (by date) as part of archiving? That's a legitimate single-node technique that aids both archiving and query performance. I can mention it as part of B's implementation.

## Recommendation: Plan B — stay single-node, archive audit-only records, upgrade when needed, re-evaluate in twelve months.

I would commit to **Plan B**. Here is the reasoning against your stated facts, the real costs of that choice, and the specific conditions that would flip me to Plan A.

## Why B is the right call now

**1. The storage pressure is mostly an archiving problem, not a scale problem.** You are at 70% capacity, but ~60% of stored rows are reconciliation records older than 18 months that are read only during audits. Removing those from the hot instance drops you to roughly 30–40% utilization — a healthy operating level — regardless of growth. The instance upgrade is then a second, independent lever that doubles capacity when you actually need it. Combined, archiving + one upgrade covers more than the 12-month horizon even with the two new markets doubling merchant count. Sharding, by contrast, does nothing for this: it spreads the 60% of audit rows across shards instead of removing them. You need archiving under either plan, so B is not the "easy" alternative to A — it is the direct fix for the pressure that actually exists.

**2. Sharding by merchant id attacks the wrong bottleneck and threatens your hardest requirement.** Your binding constraint is regulators requiring strict transactional consistency for ledger writes. Sharding by merchant id preserves that only for transactions touching a single merchant; anything cross-merchant (settlement totals, inter-merchant transfers, market-level reporting) becomes a distributed transaction with two-phase commit — exactly where consistency guarantees get fragile and audit stories get complicated. A single node gives you ACID trivially, which is precisely what a regulated payments ledger values most.

**3. The team and timeline are mismatched to Plan A.** Nobody has operated a sharded or distributed database, you have five engineers, and Plan A means a production migration of money movement in two quarters. That is a bet-the-company schedule: learning distributed consistency semantics on live ledger writes, under regulatory scrutiny, with no prior experience. The 12-month window of B is better spent building the archiving pipeline and — cheaply, in staging — running a sharding pilot so that a future decision is informed rather than forced.

**4. The growth numbers, after archiving, are comfortably within single-node reach.** Volume doubles every ~8 months, but that's total volume including the archival tier. The hot dataset grows far more slowly; the upgrade doubles hot capacity; and merchant count doubling doesn't linearly multiply per-merchant ledger volume. Nothing in your facts says you are near a throughput ceiling today — the stated problem is capacity utilization, which B solves directly.

## Real costs and risks of B (be honest about them)

- **The archiving pipeline is real work with regulatory teeth.** You must extract, move, and — critically — keep audit records durable, immutable, and retrievable within audit timelines. The risk isn't the move; it's the retrieval path: if an audit needs an 18-month-old reconciliation record and it now lives in cold storage, retrieval latency and tooling become your compliance exposure. Budget explicitly for an audit-retrieval workflow and test it against a regulator-style query, not just a storage dump. Consider native PostgreSQL range partitioning by date as part of this — it makes the archive cut and the hot table's query performance cleaner without any distributed complexity.
- **The upgrade is not free.** The larger instance roughly doubles compute/storage spend, and resizing typically means a maintenance window / brief downtime — plan it like the regulated event it is. Also, one upgrade is only one rung: after it, you've consumed your headroom and the next decision has less slack.
- **You will be running closer to operational limits than a sharded fleet would.** Monitor bloat, vacuum, connections, and IOPS; 70% utilization invites bloat-driven surprises if maintenance isn't disciplined.
- **Deferral risk.** If growth accelerates beyond projections — say new markets bring far more than 2x, or a workload shift drives write-throughput saturation — you face the sharding decision a year from now under more pressure and with less runway. That is the genuine cost of choosing B, and it's why the re-evaluation must be a scheduled, owned commitment, not a hope.

## Conditions under which Plan A becomes the right choice

Flip to A when any of these hold:

1. **Throughput, not storage, becomes the binding constraint** — sustained TPS/write-latency saturation on the largest acceptable instance, with CPU/IO at ceiling and volume still doubling.
2. **Post-archive growth stays steep** — the hot dataset keeps doubling every ~8 months even after the 60% archival cut, and you've consumed the instance ladder (no higher rung, or the next rung is a cost cliff).
3. **The workload partitions cleanly by merchant** — you can enforce that essentially all transactions are single-merchant (cross-merchant operations are rare and can be routed to a coordinating path), making the shard key safe rather than wishful.
4. **The team acquires distributed experience** — a hire or a trained, successful Citus-style pilot in staging running real ledger workloads for 3–6 months, so the migration isn't a first-time lesson on production money movement.
5. **Archiving stops working as a tool** — e.g., audits increasingly need the "cold" data hot, retrieval SLAs can't be met from archival storage, or a regulator requires near-real-time access to records you'd otherwise age out.

Also note the cheaper middle option that may make A unnecessary for years: if you ever hit single-node limits, **native PostgreSQL partitioning by date plus archiving** buys headroom without any distributed system — worth trying before committing to sharding, since it keeps ACID trivially.

**Bottom line:** B fixes the problem you actually have (capacity driven by dead audit rows), protects the consistency requirement you can't compromise, and fits the team you have. Commit to B, build the archive and audit-retrieval path properly, schedule the upgrade deliberately, run a sharding pilot in staging over the year, and re-evaluate with data — not fear — in twelve months.

Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 no such job, S216 kill/signal delivery failure.","function_id":"shell::kill","worker_name":"shell"},{"description":"List background jobs (running + recently completed). Takes no arguments.","function_id":"shell::list","worker_name":"shell"},{"description":"Fetch the full record (status, exit_code, timing) of a background job by job_id. Errors return { code, message }; common: S211 no such job.","function_id":"shell::status","worker_name":"shell"},{"description":"Console-only workspace picker control plane: list child directories under an existing host directory. Returns canonical paths and never returns files.","function_id":"shell::workspace::list","worker_name":"shell"},{"description":"Console-only workspace picker control plane: return canonical host directory anchors that an operator can browse before choosing a per-session working directory.","function_id":"shell::workspace::roots","worker_name":"shell"},{"description":"Console-only workspace picker control plane: validate that `path` is an existing host directory and return its canonical path.","function_id":"shell::workspace::validate","worker_name":"shell"},{"description":"Fan-in gate: record one arrival against a barrier and answer the typed condition decision — `skip` until the expected set has arrived, then `allow` EXACTLY ONCE carrying every arrival's payload.
